lead: Paul begins with a blessing that comes out of real suffering: the God of all consolation comforts us so that we can comfort others. The Gospel speaks of a gift with no limit: the Spirit is given “without measure”. Consolation that passes from person to person, and a Spirit that never runs out, make a fitting pair for the memory of Mar Gregorios of Nyssa, who taught that the soul never stops growing toward God.

set: Paul's relations with the Corinthians have been painful. He has written them a letter “with many tears” (2:4), and has been waiting anxiously for news. His letters usually open with a thanksgiving; here he opens with a blessing of God, in the form of Jewish prayer. He writes as a man who has lately been close to death.
str: vv. 3–4: God consoles us so that we can console others.
vv. 5–7: suffering and consolation are shared between Paul and the Church.
vv. 8–9: the affliction in Asia, and what it taught him.
vv. 10–11: God will rescue again, and your prayers help.
kw: Comfort that also strengthens, from a word meaning to call someone to one's side. The word and its verb come again and again in these verses, as the English “console” and “consolation” show. John's Gospel calls the Holy Spirit by a related name, the Paraclete (John 14:16).
Literally pressure, being pressed or crushed. Paul uses the same picture in v. 8: “crushed”.
An official verdict. What happened to Paul in the Roman province of Asia, whose chief city was Ephesus, he does not say, and scholars can only guess.
vv: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and the God of all consolation,
“Father of mercies” is a phrase at home in Jewish prayer. A man who has just despaired of life begins by praising God.
who consoles us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to console those who are in any affliction
Consolation is not for keeping. A wound that God has healed can become a way of helping others. Those who have suffered often know what to say, and when to say nothing.
so that we would rely not on ourselves but on God who raises the dead.
Paul sees a purpose in the worst of it. When every human support is gone, only the God of the Resurrection remains.
as you also join in helping us by your prayers,
The great apostle says that he needs the prayers of the Church he has quarrelled with. Prayer binds the Church together even when relations are hard.
ch: The Catechism says that blessing is the basic movement of Christian prayer (CCC 2626) and points to Paul's own life as an example of intercession in the first Christian communities (CCC 2636). It teaches that suffering united with Christ becomes a sharing in his saving work (CCC 1521). The Church's anointing of the sick is one sign that God's consolation comes through the hands of others.

r.h: He gives the Spirit without measure
set: John the Baptist has just said of Jesus, “He must increase, but I must decrease” (3:30). The verses that follow could be the Baptist still speaking, or the evangelist reflecting on the scene. The Greek has no quotation marks, and commentators differ. Either way, they sum up the whole of chapter 3, with its themes of being born from above, testimony and life.
str: v. 31: the one from above and the one from the earth.
vv. 32–33: his testimony, and those who accept it.
vv. 34–35: God's words, the Spirit, and all things in the Son's hands.
v. 36: the choice between life and wrath.
kw: The same word Jesus used to Nicodemus (3:3, 7), where it also means “again”. The one who comes from above is the one who gives birth from above.

Literally “not from a measure”, as one measures out grain. The Greek of v. 34 does not state the subject: God gives the Spirit to the Son, or the Son gives the Spirit to us. The POC names God as the giver: “ദൈവം അളന്നല്ല ആത്മാവിനെ കൊടുക്കുന്നത്”.
Verse 33 uses the word for setting one's seal on a document: whoever accepts the testimony puts his own signature to the truth of God.
vv: Whoever has accepted his testimony has certified this, that God is true.
Faith is not a guess. It is a personal signature, a word of trust in the God who speaks.
He whom God has sent speaks the words of God, for he gives the Spirit without measure.
The prophets each received a gift for a task. Jesus has the Spirit in fullness, and from that fullness he gives.
Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; whoever disobeys the Son will not see life, but must endure God’s wrath.

In John eternal life begins now, as a present gift: “has”. God's “wrath” is not a fit of temper; it describes the state of one who refuses life. The verse is a warning given so that a person may turn.
ch: The Catechism quotes this Gospel when it teaches that from the moment of his conception the humanity of Christ is filled with the Holy Spirit, for God gives him the Spirit without measure (CCC 504). It adds that from his fullness we have all received. It also cites this passage when it speaks of the need of faith for salvation (CCC 161).

rite: Mar Gregorios of Nyssa (fourth century) was the younger brother of Mar Baselios, and one of the great Cappadocian Fathers. As a bishop he defended the faith of Nicaea on the Trinity. In his Life of Moses he taught that the soul, drawn on by God who has no limit, never reaches an end of its growth, and that each discovery opens a greater longing (in substance). A Spirit given “without measure” is the Gospel root of that teaching.
study: Whom has God placed near me who needs the consolation I once received?
Where has God's gift to me become smaller only because my longing has become smaller?
